title: Vailankanni (India)
hookLine: a coastal shrine of Our Lady of Good Health, loved by people of many religions

lines: ON HER KNEES TOWARD A WHITE CHURCH.
A WAX LEG FOR A BAD KNEE.
ONE SHORE, PILGRIMS OF MANY FAITHS.
cards: On the beach, a woman in a yellow sari is making her way toward a white church on her knees. Behind her, a father carries a little boy whose head has just been shaved, an offering for a fever that broke.
At a stall nearby, someone buys a small wax model of a leg, to leave at the altar for a knee that won't heal. Some pilgrims are Catholic, some Hindu, some Muslim.
They've all come to the same shore in the south of India, to a mother they call Our Lady of Good Health.

teach.b: Start with the stories, which come from tradition rather than any record. Tradition says a boy carrying milk to a customer stopped to rest under a tree, and a beautiful lady holding a child asked him for milk for her son.
He gave it, and arrived to find his pot still full. Another story tells of a lame boy selling buttermilk who was asked the same, gave, and stood up and walked.
And sailors caught in a storm are said to have promised Mary a chapel if they reached land alive. They did, and they built it.
What holds these stories together: a mother asking for something for her child, and people healed and kept safe. Next, the name.

The Litany of Loreto calls Mary health of the sick, and Vailankanni gives her almost that title. People come carrying their bodies: bad backs, failing eyes, children who won't eat, babies long hoped for.
They leave wax or metal models of the part that hurts, a kind of prayer you can hold in your hand.
In Matthew's Gospel, a sick woman pushes through a crowd toward Jesus, thinking, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch only his garment, I shall be healed."
She wanted to bring her body close.

teach.h: IF I SHALL TOUCH ONLY HIS GARMENT, I SHALL BE HEALED.
teach.b: The shrine's gates stand open, and people of other faiths come to pray there too, in their own ways. Catholics there don't check anyone at the door; they meet them as fellow pilgrims, all asking for the same plain thing.

how: Pilgrims come to the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health at Vailankanni in Tamil Nadu, India, to pray for healing, some walking on their knees or offering small models of the part of the body they hope to see healed; people of other faiths visit and pray there too.

games.q: you're a sailor in a storm off the coast of India, sure the ship is going down. what do you promise?
o: to build Mary a chapel where you land.
to never go to sea again.
games.why: tradition says sailors promised Mary a chapel if they reached land alive. they came ashore, and they built it.

practice: Rest a few breaths on one part of your body that works without your asking, then on one part that hurts, without arguing with it. Now hold someone whose health is failing just as gently.
If you pray, say a Hail Mary for them, or the litany's words, health of the sick, pray for us; if not, wish them well, by name.

wordCard.voice: Vailankanni. The town on India's southern coast where Mary is honored as Our Lady of Good Health, and pilgrims of many faiths come asking to be healed. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Litany of Loreto: health of the sick, close to Vailankanni's title, Our Lady of Good Health.

carryVoice: Your line: our lady of good health. One shore, many faiths. Same time tomorrow.
